title: The Downside of Using Exclusion to Create Group Cohesion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership field note examines the psychology of exclusion as a tool for building group cohesion—why it works, how it backfires, and why skilled leaders ultimately avoid it. Exclusion creates clear in-group identity and rapid bonding by making membership feel earned and special, and by giving the group a shared 'other' to define itself against. But over time the mechanism corrodes: members become afraid of being cast out, begin self-censoring, and stop taking risks, turning apparent cohesion into brittle compliance built on fear. The alternative is cohesion built on shared purpose and values rather than on rejection of outsiders—slower to build but producing a culture where people speak up, take risks, and remain loyal by genuine choice rather than fear of exclusion.
points: Exclusion raises the perceived value of group membership by creating scarcity and an in-group/out-group distinction—one of the fastest tools a leader has for generating cohesion.
Common forms include mocking competitors, exclusive hiring criteria, ritual-based entry, and 'us vs. them' narratives against larger or slower rivals.
Over time, exclusion-based cohesion becomes fear-based compliance: members suppress disagreement and avoid risk because crossing a line feels like risking expulsion.
The resulting brittleness means the group appears cohesive but lacks the psychological safety required for honest feedback, risk-taking, or genuine commitment.
Good leaders build belonging through shared purpose, values, and standards—a slower process that produces durable loyalty and a culture people choose to be part of.
quotes: Somewhat ironically, excluding people often creates a deeper connection and more pride in being a member. Exclusion is one of the oldest tricks in the leadership playbook, and it's worth understanding exactly how and why it works.
Nothing bonds a group faster than rejecting others or celebrating a shared sense of being chosen. That's why exclusion is so tempting for leaders in a hurry to increase group cohesion.

Over time, people start to fear being rejected by the group and excluded like the outsiders they've been taught to look down on. So, they fall in line. They become less willing to speak up about issues they disagree with, because disagreement begins to feel like disloyalty.
The very cohesion that felt so strong at the start slowly turns brittle. It holds together through fear of exclusion rather than genuine commitment.
Good leaders create belonging without making it dependent on exclusion. They resist the shortcut of an 'us' versus 'them' story, even though it is fast and effective.
The circle that holds people by fear will always be weaker than the one that holds them by choice.
